title: Endings with One Rook and Pawns
subtitle: An advanced pawn is not always a winning pawn

source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter V, §28 Endings with One Rook and Pawns, Example 59

narration.say: This ending comes from Marshall against Rosenthal, in the Manhattan Chess Club championship of 1909–1910.
Capablanca gives rook to c7, check, as the winning move. Marshall instead advances the pawn and gives Black a drawing chance.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Find the drawing defence on the sixth rank.

narration.say: White pushes f7. Black must place the rook behind the pawn.

feedback.*: Rook to d8. The rook controls f8.

exercise.hint: Rook to d8. The rook controls f8.

narration.say: Black brings the king to c4. Capablanca explains that the b-pawn gives enough counterplay to draw.
Reset to the initial position. This time Black tries checks instead of the rook defence on d8.
The white king approaches and the rook gains a useful tempo.
White has improved the king and rook. The book contrasts this with the drawing defence Rd8.

steps.title: Variation: make room for the king

narration.say: Reset again. After f7, Black instead plays rook to f6.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Clear the h-file and keep the rook active.

narration.say: White advances h4. Black advances the b-pawn, but White gains time with rook checks.
Capablanca explains that White can now attack the b-pawn or bring the rook to f3, reaching a favourable ending.
After f6 and f7, Black needs accurate rook placement. Routine checks can help the opposing king advance.
We have kept the variations separate by resetting the board. Each branch illustrates a different defensive choice.
